messages.subject: Posterior of the mixture component
parts:
Hi guys, sorry to bug the group but I can't figure this out from the docs or searching the mailing list.

I have count data across some regions and through time and the model I'm implementing is attempting to identify abnormal temporal trends (this but without using the BUGS cut function). The model works by modelling the counts as log poisson with a rate parameter which is a mixture of two rate parameters, 

Model 1: where we have smoothed spatial component and a general temporal trend - assuming space-time separability and

Model 2: which has a separate temporal trend for each region. 

We set the mixture component to have 95% of the regions follow model 1 and 5% the other. I've written the model and it runs fine, but I have no idea how to obtain the posterior of the mixture component for each region - or at least some classification method to assign 5% of regions as those which are most likely to have been one of the regions that had an abnormal temporal trend (followed model 2). 

Also, I get the 

Informational Message: The current Metropolis proposal is about to be rejected because of the following issue:

validate transformed params: mu_specific[1117] is -0.00154563, but must be greater than or equal to 0
If this warning occurs sporadically, such as for highly constrained variable types like covariance matrices, then the sampler is fine,
but if this warning occurs often then your model may be either severely ill-conditioned or misspecified.

warning hundreds/thousands of times during the sampling. It's always one of the rate parameters being very slightly below zero - any reason to be concerned with the fit because of this?

Here's the stan code for the model so far,

functions {
  /**
  * This part is taken from Max Joseph's write-up here: http://mc-stan.org/documentation/case-studies/mbjoseph-CARStan.html
  *
  * Return the log probability of a proper conditional autoregressive (CAR) prior
  * with a sparse representation for the adjacency matrix
  *
  * @param phi Vector containing the parameters with a CAR prior
  * @param tau Precision parameter for the CAR prior (real)
  * @param alpha Dependence (usually spatial) parameter for the CAR prior (real)
  * @param W_sparse Sparse representation of adjacency matrix (int array)
  * @param n Length of phi (int)
  * @param W_n Number of adjacent pairs (int)
  * @param D_sparse Number of neighbors for each location (vector)
  * @param lambda Eigenvalues of D^{-1/2}*W*D^{-1/2} (vector)
  *
  * @return Log probability density of CAR prior up to additive constant
  */
  real sparse_car_lpdf(vector phi, real tau, real alpha,
    int[,] W_sparse, vector D_sparse, vector lambda, int n, int W_n) {
      row_vector[n] phit_D; // phi' * D
      row_vector[n] phit_W; // phi' * W
      vector[n] ldet_terms;
   
      phit_D = (phi .* D_sparse)';
      phit_W = rep_row_vector(0, n);
      for (i in 1:W_n) {
        phit_W[W_sparse[i, 1]] = phit_W[W_sparse[i, 1]] + phi[W_sparse[i, 2]];
        phit_W[W_sparse[i, 2]] = phit_W[W_sparse[i, 2]] + phi[W_sparse[i, 1]];
      }
   
      for (i in 1:n) ldet_terms[i] = log1m(alpha * lambda[i]);
      return 0.5 * (n * log(tau)
                    + sum(ldet_terms)
                    - tau * (phit_D * phi - alpha * (phit_W * phi)));
  }
}
data {
    int<lower = 1> numRegions; // The number of regions
    int<lower = 1> nt; // The number of time points
    // matrix[numRegions, nt] observed;  // The observed counts at each point
    int observed[numRegions, nt];
    vector[numRegions] log_expected; // The expected number of counts based on demographics etc
    matrix<lower = 0, upper = 1>[numRegions, numRegions] W; // The adjacency matrix
    int W_n;
    real<lower=0, upper=1> alpha;
    real<lower=0, upper=1> prop_unusual;
}
transformed data{
    int W_sparse[W_n, 2];   // adjacency pairs
    vector[numRegions] D_sparse;     // diagonal of D (number of neigbors for each site)
    vector[numRegions] lambda;       // eigenvalues of invsqrtD * W * invsqrtD
   
    { // generate sparse representation for W
 int counter;
 counter = 1;
 // loop over upper triangular part of W to identify neighbor pairs
 for (i in 1:(numRegions - 1)) {
    for (j in (i + 1):numRegions) {
 if (W[i, j] == 1) {
    W_sparse[counter, 1] = i;
    W_sparse[counter, 2] = j;
    counter = counter + 1;
 }
    }
 }
    }
    for (i in 1:numRegions) D_sparse[i] = sum(W[i]);
    {
 vector[numRegions] invsqrtD;  
 for (i in 1:numRegions) {
    invsqrtD[i] = 1 / sqrt(D_sparse[i]);
 }
 lambda = eigenvalues_sym(quad_form(W, diag_matrix(invsqrtD)));
    }
}
parameters {
    vector[nt] temporal;
    vector[numRegions] v; // Spatial smoothing component
    vector[numRegions] lmbda;
    real<lower = 0> sigma_v; // Variance of spatial component, v
    real<lower = 0> sigma_temporal; // Variance of temporal component
    real<lower = 0> sigma_l;
    real<lower = 0> var_ind_temporal[numRegions]; // The variance of the individual temporal trends
    // real<lower = 0, upper = 1> alpha; // The degree of spatial dependence
   
    matrix[numRegions, nt] ind_temporal; // The temporal trend of an individual region
    vector[numRegions] ind_constant;


    real constant;


    real a;
    real<lower = 0> b;
}
transformed parameters {
    matrix<lower = 0>[numRegions, nt] mu_general;
    matrix<lower = 0>[numRegions, nt] mu_specific;
   
    mu_general = rep_matrix(temporal, numRegions)' + rep_matrix(lmbda, nt) + rep_matrix(log_expected, nt) + rep_matrix(constant, numRegions, nt);
    mu_specific = ind_temporal + rep_matrix(ind_constant, nt) + rep_matrix(log_expected, nt);
   
}
model {
    sigma_temporal ~ normal(0, 1);
    sigma_v ~ normal(0, 1);
    sigma_l ~ normal(0, 1);
   
    temporal[1] ~ normal(0, sigma_temporal); // 1d random walk prior on temporal component
    ind_temporal[,1] ~ normal(0, sqrt(var_ind_temporal));
    for (t in 2:nt) {
       temporal[t] ~ normal(temporal[t - 1], sigma_temporal);
       ind_temporal[,t] ~ normal(ind_temporal[, t - 1], sqrt(var_ind_temporal));
    }


    ind_constant ~ normal(0, 30); // non-informative prior on the constant term per region
    constant ~ normal(0, 30); // constant term for  


    var_ind_temporal ~ lognormal(a, b);
    a ~ normal(0, 30);
    b ~ normal(0, 2.5);
   
    v ~ sparse_car(sigma_v, alpha, W_sparse, D_sparse, lambda, numRegions, W_n);
    lmbda ~ normal(v, sigma_l);


    for (i in 1:numRegions){
       target += log_sum_exp(log(1.0 - prop_unusual) + poisson_log_lpmf(observed[i,] | mu_general[i,]),
                             log(prop_unusual) + poisson_log_lpmf(observed[i,] | mu_specific[i,]));
    }


}



Any help would be appreciated!

> On Jan 15, 2017, at 1:31 AM, Michael Redman <michaelal...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> Hi guys, sorry to bug the group but I can't figure this out from the docs or searching the mailing list.
>

> I have count data across at some regions and through time and the model I'm implementing is attempting to identify abnormal temporal trends (this but without using the BUGS cut function).

The only way to get cut-like behavior is to put the stuff that's cut
out in generated quantities. The BUGS approach isn't a Bayesian one.
> The model works by modelling the counts as log poisson

I don't know what that means. I know the Poisson distribution for
counts.

> with a rate parameter which is a mixture of two rate parameters,
>
> Model 1: where we have smoothed spatial component and a general temporal trend - assuming space-time separability and
>
> Model 2: which has a separate temporal trend for each region.
>
> We set the mixture component to have 95% of the regions follow model 1 and 5% the other. I've written the model and it runs fine, but I have no idea how to obtain the posterior of the mixture component for each region - or at least some classification method to assign 5% of regions as those which are most likely to have been one of the regions that had an abnormal temporal trend (followed model 2).

Usually you want the data to set the ratio of mixing. But even
if you fix it, suppose you have a model which is

p(y | ...) = 0.95 * foo(y | ...) + 0.05 * bar(y | ...)

where you're really thinking this is true mixture with z being
a discrete responsibility parameter:

z ~ bernoulli(0.95)
p(y | ...) = foo(y | ...) if z = 1
bar(y | ...) if z = 0


In Stan, that's

target += log_sum_exp(log(0.95) + foo_lpdf(y | ...),
log(0.05) + bar_lpdf(y | ...));

So what you want is

Pr[z = 1 | y]

The way to compute that is defined in the manual section on mixtures.

Pr[z = 1 | y] = 0.95 * foo(y | ...) / (0.95 * foo(y | ...) + 0.05 * bar(y | ...))

You probably want to stay on the log scale and compute

log Pr[z = 1 | y]

which is

log(log(0.95) + foo_lpdf(y | ...))
- log_sum_exp(log(0.95) + foo_lpdf(y | ...),
log(0.05) + bar_lpdf(y | ...));

But if you calculate log densities, then it's tricky to get an
average, because that also has to be done with log_sum_exp.
There's a discussion of that in my binary trial case study on the
case studies page on the web.

or you can just round off and deal with the inevitable rounding to
0 or 1.

- Bob

>
> Also, I get the
>
> Informational Message: The current Metropolis proposal is about to be rejected because of the following issue:
>
> validate transformed params: mu_specific[1117] is -0.00154563, but must be greater than or equal to 0
> If this warning occurs sporadically, such as for highly constrained variable types like covariance matrices, then the sampler is fine,
> but if this warning occurs often then your model may be either severely ill-conditioned or misspecified.
>
> warning hundreds/thousands of times during the sampling. It's always one of the rate parameters being very slightly below zero - any reason to be concerned with the fit because of this?

Yes. You need to constrain the rate parameter to have <lower=0> either
directly or indirectly. Every valid parameter vector that satisfies
the declared constraints should have a finite log density.

- Bob
